items.exemplar: (a) Liberals saw federal power as the tool for economic security and social justice, while Reagan's conservatism saw it as a threat to freedom and growth — opposite answers to what government is for. (b) The 1981 tax cuts expressed this by treating lower taxes as the engine of growth: the premise was that Washington taking less would unleash private enterprise, reversing the liberal premise that Washington should tax and spend to manage the economy. (c) Clinton, a Democrat, declaring 'the era of big government is over' and signing welfare reform shows the shift's durability — the opposition party was now governing on conservative premises.
items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — 'Compare Reagan's conservatism with the liberalism it displaced'; §The story — 1980 'repudiation'; Clinton triangulation

parts.prompt: Identify ONE difference between Reagan's conservatism and the New Deal/Great Society liberalism it displaced, in their views of federal power.
Explain how ONE Reagan policy — the 1981 tax cuts, deregulation, or the PATCO firings — expressed the conservative view identified in part (a).
Explain how ONE development of the 1990s shows that Reagan's conservative shift outlasted his presidency.

items.stimulus_text: The New Deal and Great Society built a federal government that regulated business, taxed progressively to fund social programs, and acted as the guarantor of economic security. Ronald Reagan's 1980 victory repudiated that premise: he promised to cut taxes, slash regulation, and shrink domestic government while rebuilding the military. (Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md.)

items.attribution: Original stimulus composed for this item; figures approximate, per u9.md §The story.
items.exemplar: (a) The theory predicted that lower taxes would unleash private-sector growth large enough to generate the revenue to pay for the cuts themselves. (b) The deficit roughly tripled between 1980 and 1986, showing the prediction failed in the short run: growth returned but revenues never caught up with the lower rates. (c) The 1981 tax cuts reduced revenue while the military buildup sharply raised spending, and domestic cuts could not cover the combined gap — so the deficit grew despite expansion.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — '"Reaganomics" rested on supply-side theory: lower taxes would unleash growth that paid for itself. Growth did return, but so did huge deficits and stark inequality'; §Key terms — Reaganomics

parts.prompt: Identify the central prediction of supply-side theory as described in the stimulus.
Explain what the deficit figures in the stimulus show about that prediction.
Explain ONE reason the deficits grew even though the economy was expanding.

items.stimulus_text: Supply-side theory promised that the 1981 tax cuts would unleash enough growth to pay for themselves. The federal deficit instead rose from $74 billion in 1980 to $221 billion in 1986, while the economy grew and inequality widened. (Original stimulus composed for this item; figures approximate, per u9.md §The story.)

items.exemplar: (a) The stagnation of the Soviet command economy — which could not innovate or match Western productivity — left the system brittle; Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika then unleashed nationalist and democratic forces he could not control. (b) Reagan's military buildup, including SDI, forced Moscow into an arms race its struggling economy could not afford, deepening the fiscal crisis. (c) Neither cause works alone: American pressure mattered because it pressed on a system already rotting from within — a healthy USSR could have absorbed the buildup, and internal decay alone might have produced reform rather than collapse without the external strain.
items.fact_source: u9.md §What the exam tests here — 'the exam rewards multi-causal answers — internal Soviet decay and Gorbachev's reforms alongside American pressure (the military buildup, SDI) — not single-hero stories'

parts.prompt: Identify ONE internal Soviet cause of the USSR's collapse.
Identify ONE way American pressure contributed to the collapse.
Explain why historians favor a multi-causal explanation rather than crediting a single cause.

items.stimulus_text: The Cold War ended with the Berlin Wall's fall in November 1989, German reunification in 1990, and the Soviet Union's dissolution in December 1991. Historians debate how much credit belongs to American pressure — the military buildup, SDI, Reagan's confrontation — versus internal Soviet decay and Gorbachev's reforms. (Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md.)

items.attribution: Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md §The story.
items.exemplar: (a) The foreign-born share of the population nearly tripled (about 4.7 to 13.7 percent), and the regional origins shifted from mostly European to mostly Latin American and Asian. (b) The law prioritized relatives of citizens and residents, so each admitted immigrant could sponsor family members who could then sponsor their own — a chain-migration multiplier that compounded across decades. (c) Like the Know-Nothings of the 1850s and the 1920s restrictionists, modern nativists argued newcomers threatened American jobs, culture, and political stability — the same structure of argument aimed at different groups.
items.fact_source: u9.md §The story — 'demographic change — the coming "majority-minority" nation — reshaped politics, especially around immigration'; 2016 backlash 'against immigration'

parts.prompt: Describe ONE demographic change in American immigration between 1970 and 2020.
Explain how the 1965 law's family-reunification rules produced a decades-long 'long tail' of growing immigration.
Explain ONE continuity between the nativist backlash of the 1990s–2000s and an earlier nativist episode in American history.

items.stimulus_text: After the 1965 immigration law replaced the 1920s quota system, the foreign-born share of the U.S. population nearly tripled between 1970 and 2020, and newcomers came increasingly from Latin America and Asia rather than Europe. The review says this demographic change 'reshaped politics, especially around immigration,' and that the 2016 election channeled a backlash against immigration. (Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md.)

items.attribution: Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md §Key terms and §What the exam tests here.
items.exemplar: (a) The act expanded federal surveillance powers — including wiretaps, records searches, and detention authority — beyond their pre-9/11 limits. (b) Supporters argued extraordinary powers were necessary to stop another 9/11, while critics warned that emergency powers erode civil liberties and become permanent — the recurring American tension between security and liberty. (c) Like the Espionage Act of 1917, which jailed dissenters during World War I, the Patriot Act used a crisis to widen the state's reach at liberty's expense; both were later narrowed and reckoned with, showing the pattern of crisis, expansion, and eventual correction.
items.fact_source: u9.md §Key terms — Patriot Act (2001); §What the exam tests here — 'Compare 9/11's aftermath with earlier wartime expansions of federal power'

parts.prompt: Identify ONE way the Patriot Act expanded federal power after 9/11.
Explain the security-versus-liberty debate the act provoked.
Compare the Patriot Act's expansion of federal power with ONE earlier wartime expansion, such as the Espionage Act, internment, or McCarthyism.

items.stimulus_text: After September 11, 2001, Congress passed the Patriot Act, expanding federal surveillance and detention powers. Supporters called the powers necessary to prevent another attack; critics warned they eroded civil liberties. Earlier crises had produced similar expansions: the Espionage Act of 1917, Japanese internment in 1942, and McCarthyism in the 1950s. (Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md.)

items.attribution: Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md §The story.
items.exemplar: (a) The housing bubble: risky mortgages and speculative buying drove home prices to unsustainable levels, and financial engineering spread mortgage risk through securities held across the system. (b) Taxpayers rescued the financial firms whose recklessness caused the crisis while ordinary homeowners facing foreclosure got far less help — it looked like failure was being rewarded, fueling populist fury on both sides. (c) In 2008 the government intervened massively and quickly through TARP and other rescues, while in the early 1930s federal action was limited and late; the 2008 response reflected lessons learned from the Depression's deepening through inaction.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE cause of the Great Recession of 2007–2009.
Explain why the TARP bank bailouts angered the public despite stabilizing the financial system.
Compare the federal response to the 2008 crisis with the federal response to the early years of the Great Depression.

items.stimulus_text: The housing bubble's collapse in 2008 produced the worst financial crisis since the Depression. The government's bank bailouts (TARP) saved the financial system but fed a populist fury on both left and right. (Original stimulus composed for this item, summarizing u9.md §The story.)
